utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Circumstances in relation to the application of Rule 15 bis are unchanged, which means that we'll continue to hear this case by two Judges; Judge Fluegge for urgent personal reasons unable to continue to hear the case for the moment. I can already inform the parties that the expectation is that Judge Fluegge will be back with us next week, Tuesday. No preliminaries? Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. Good morning. We would like to call Mr. Malcic, Stojan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Malcic be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Malcic. Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Malcic. Mr. Malcic, you will first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Malcic.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just ask for the help from the usher, and I would like to give clean statement to the witness so he has it in front of him. Would he be so kind and show it to the Prosecution first. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Malcic, we need to make certain corrections first in your statement. First of all, for the record, would you please say --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm getting signals that there is no sound in the court reporter's headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Shall we try again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can everyone hear me now who needs to hear me. Yes, it seems to be okay. No one is crying or jumping up. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try again in B/C/S to see if everyone is getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still no translation, I can see. [Interpretation] Can we try again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could hear the English booth, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think we need your help, if you could speak a few words in B/C/S, then we can see whether it all works.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, to test, the system again, are you getting any interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do, but the transcriber does not, as far as I can see. The problem apparently is that words spoken in English are understood, but as soon as the English words come from the interpreter booth interpreting what Mr. Lukic says, then it goes wrong. We'll have to -- we'll wait for one or two minutes to see whether it can be quickly resolved. If not, we'll take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The court reporter still doesn't hear the English booth. I must admit that for me also hearing my own voice through the microphone comes a bit later than usual. We'll take a short break and see whether the matter can be resolved. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We have a technical problem, Mr. Malcic, so we have to fix it first before we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a short break. Everyone is invited to remain standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Apparently the technical problems have been resolved, Mr. Lukic, so whenever you talk in B/C/S then we'll be able to hear what you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technical problems have been resolved, Mr. Malcic; therefore, we can continue. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Malcic, would you please state for the record your name, your full name.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Stojan Malcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you given a statement to the Defence team of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall now go through certain corrections that need to be made. There are several typographic errors. Let us look at paragraph 12 -- [In English] 2, sorry. [Interpretation] Paragraph 2. In this paragraph, it is said that you were retired on 31st January 1997. Which date is correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: On 31st January 1997, I went on sick-leave, and I stopped with active military service on 31st August 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, in paragraph 30, the last sentence containing the date is correct because paragraph 30 states that: "This witness was retired on 31st August 1997."

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 17 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't call this on our screens. If we can have 1D01717 on our screens, please. And we need paragraph 17; it's page 6. [Interpretation] Only in the B/C/S version, it says: "Approximately on 30th May 1992, I became a member of the VRS." It's obvious that 1992 is the correct year, not 2992 as it is stated in the Serbian version. Then we need paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1, Mr. Malcic, in the English version your year of birth is different. Is the B/C/S version correct that you were born on the 1st of February, 1948?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the English version that says you were born in 1942 needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 6 is on the next page in both versions. Again, the two versions differ. In the year when this witness was released from prison, the B/C/S version is correct. The year is 1992 and in English, we read 1995. But I will ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you released? On the 13th of May which year?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I was exchanged on 13 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, before that 1992, it says: "I was arrested on the 3rd of May, 1992 and released on the 13th May 1992, which is not true." Oh, okay. "My arrest occurred on the 6th." Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to paragraph 17 again. That is the only real correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One word has been omitted. It says: "As part of this function, I was not a member of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska but I did attend meetings of the collegium." The wording should be -- but I will ask the witness. Were you a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Main Staff but I was not a member of the collegium of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will then read the proper wording of this passage in paragraph 17. "[In English]: The function I performed did not make me a member of the collegium of the Main Staff of the VRS, but I attended their collegiums in cases when the Main Staff decided on the matters concerning the status of professional officers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the new wording? But the witness said the other thing a minute ago. "I was a member of the Main Staff but I was not a member of the collegium of the Main Staff." Now you say: "The function I performed did not make me a member of the collegium of the Main Staff." Yes. Okay. Fine. Yes. No, I missed it. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, let us look at the first page of this statement again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] If we can see the cover page, please, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Malcic, you have it in hard copy and also on the screen before you. Do you see the signature?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let us look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see the signature there?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After these corrections, do you believe the statement you gave to the Defence team of General Mladic to be correct and truthful?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: This statement is correct and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions that I and my investigators asked you before, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would give exactly the same answers, perhaps in even more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should now like to tender the statement of Mr. Malcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1717 receives number D656, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D656 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the short summary of this witness's statement. [In English] Stojan Malcic was active officer serving in garrison Sarajevo from 1971 until the 3rd May of 1992 when he was arrested by the Muslim police in Sarajevo. After his release from prison on 13th of May, 1992, he went to the Serb territory. The torture he suffered in prison has left him with permanent health injuries. He was retired on 31st January 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 31st August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, exactly. I have the same mistake. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was retired -- the witness intervened as well. He was retired in August 31st, 1997. In May 1992, an order was issued that all JNA units should return to Serbia, except for the officers and soldiers born in B and H. They were ordered to stay in B and H. After the formation of VRS, it continued to apply all rules and laws of JNA. On 30th of May, 1992, the Main Staff VRS assumed the office, followed by the Order from 16th of June, 1992. Malcic's duty, among others, was to deal with the salaries of the active officers, but not with the salaries of the reserve officers and soldiers who were paid by the RS or municipal authorities. Malcic states that the documents concerning the status of the former JNA officers show that their stay in B and H was voluntary and they were given the possibility to choose. The aim of the named order was to protect the officers at the given period. His office did not receive this document. At that time, there was a growing distrust among reserve officers of different ethnicities. Also, the distrust of Serb officers was evident. They were called "commies," and the distrust culminated at the time of the JNA withdrawal into Serbia. The first information about the Srebrenica events in 1995 he received from the media. He will testify that all military operations were carried out in accordance with the rules, and that he never heard that General Mladic ordered killings of civilians or prisoners of war. And this concludes short statement summary. I do not have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that we can move on. However, one thing, Mr. Lukic, in your summary, you say it, and I also see it in the statement, "I hereby state that all the fights led by the VRS were conducted in accordance to international rules. I hope that you are aware that this the kind of sweeping statements which do not, in any way, assist the Chamber. I hope that you are aware of that. It's just -- well, I will not further say anything. Basis of knowledge, it's almost impossible to know so it would need a huge explanation, but I take it that it's just opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is just the opinion since this gentleman was never in the field --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he can state whatever he wants but he has no knowledge, and witnesses are here to tell us about their knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not about their opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he was in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even then, Mr. Lukic, take yourself seriously, this is when I refer to sweeping statements now and then. This is a beautiful example of a totally useless sweeping statement. I'm only talking about this line. Please proceed. Witness, I gave some comments as you may have heard on your statement, especially where it reads that you state that "all the fights led by the VRS were conducted in accordance with international rules," which is not easy for us to understand how such a broad, thorough, complete knowledge would be with you. You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Malcic.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malcic, as a personnel officer in the Main Staff of the VRS, part of your responsibilities included the filing of performance appraisals of generals in the VRS; yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mladic reduce the volume of his voice so that it doesn't disturb the examination of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, did you get my question or shall I repeat it for you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think I understood the question. Yes, among other things, it was my responsibility to provide official performance appraisals for military officers, with the exception of generals, in personnel files. That was done for generals by my superior, Petar --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, you mentioned your superior, and we got the first name Petar and the interpreters were not able to catch the second name. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Petar Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. So it's correct that you are -- you were familiar with the format of these performance appraisals; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it's correct that officers were regularly assessed every four years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: According to the rule book on appraisals, regular assessments are made every four years and, if necessary, they can be provided more often within one year from the previous official assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a few of these performance appraisals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P2631 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, coming up on the screen before you is the performance appraisal for Radoslav Krstic. Now, if I can focus your attention on the top right side of the -- of this document, we see that the date of the appraisal is the 6th of November, 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page, please, in each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, we see on this last page the name of General Krstic on the left side and a signature below it and the name of General Mladic on the right side and his signature below that. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So this is an appraisal for General Krstic that's being carried out by General Mladic; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malcic, below the date on the top right side of the screen, we see an evaluation period of 6 November 1991 to 6 November 1995. Now, is this an example of a regular assessment?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to the second page in each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malcic, I would like to focus your attention on the fifth sentence in this section, in this description and conclusion. It begins with the words: "As the commander of the Drina Corps, he planned, organised, and commanded the ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page just in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: " ... operations for the liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa with great success, which he carried out brilliantly, despite the fact the NATO Air Forces were directly protecting the Muslim formations." Going to the last sentence in this paragraph, we read: "According to all the contributions he made in the course of his career, and especially during the war, General Krstic is one of the most successful and most promising generals of the Serbian people." And we see below that that he is graded excellent. Now, Mr. Malcic, in terms of the actual appraisal process, would General Mladic's comments on General Krstic's actions in Srebrenica be based solely on his firsthand experience of what he could see and observe of General Krstic in Srebrenica, or would you expect him to also solicit input from General Krstic's fellow officers who are also present there during those days in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I kept records, that is to say, personnel files, of military officers up to the rank of colonel. Above that, these records and files were kept by my superior. The assessment consists of a descriptive part and a numerical part containing grades, that is, the system of grading the military officers of the JNA, which we also used in the Army of Republika Srpska because our own rule book had not been adopted yet. I cannot answer your question because I took no part in the writing of this assessment, and I do not know on what basis General Mladic provided this descriptive assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In terms of the format of this particular appraisal, is it in the same format as the appraisals that you did handle from the level of colonel downwards?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: It is the same prescribed format in which official appraisals were written for all military officers and generals in the JNA and that format we took over in the Army of Republika Srpska and applied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And would you expect the process, the appraisal process, to be the same for generals as it was for colonels downwards, the appraisals that you actually dealt with?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The answers to the questions contained in this form are exactly the same. It only depends on the superior officer how he will write and how he will fill in the form. Of course, the first page were official personnel details were filled in by my superior for generals, and it was signed off by the personnel officer of the unit in which the officer served.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to take to look at another appraisal in the same format as the one that we've just looked at. Could we please see P5023 -- forgive me, P5023.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malcic, coming up on the screen before you is the appraisal of Dragomir Milosevic. Now, again, looking at the top right of the screen, we see the date of the assessment is the 8th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can please go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see that it's been signed by General Mladic and General Milosevic. So, Mr. Malcic, this is an appraisal of Dragomir Milosevic by General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go back one page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Again, I'd like to take a look at some of the comments in this descriptive assessment and conclusion. Could we go down the page in the English a little bit, please. Sorry -- so I can see the bottom of the page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, we read: "He contributed greatly to stabilising the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which has grown under his command into a very effective operational formation and has demonstrated its strength and power by smashing many Muslim offensives towards Sarajevo, particularly in the last Muslim-NATO offensive which ended in the total defeat of the enemy which gave up pursuing their goals as a result of the enormous casualties. He has carried out all tasks skillfully and professionally, with ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go over the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: " ... great self-sacrifice and personal renunciation." And, again, we see that his performance is assessed as excellent. Now, Mr. Malcic, I mentioned that -- and we saw that the date of this assessment is the 8th of June, 1992, yet we see the date at the end is the 30th of October, 1995, and the assessment clearly covers the period when General Milosevic was commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps during 1994 and 1995. Now, as a personnel officer in the Main Staff, can you explain why the appraisal is dated 1992 but, in fact, covers a period up to October 1995?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that because I did not take part in writing this assessment in any way. I did not give my opinion or proposal. I told you how things are written up for generals.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. We can barely understand him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness, could you speak more in the microphone - we'll try to adjust it - because the interpreters have difficulties in hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Malcic. I understand that you were not privy to the content of this particular appraisal, or the last one, but I thought you might be able to help me with the actual process but it sounds as though you can't on this particular issue, so I will leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're at break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Jeremy. I'm just looking exactly at that point that's the cover page where the date range is expressed 8th of June, 1988 to 8th of June 1992. In the translation, I see 20th of July, 1992. I have some difficulties in finding that but perhaps I should zoom out a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, I think you're right, Your Honour. It actually in the translation, it's -- it is 20 July 1992. It's in evidence but it would need a correction. With your leave, I'll arrange for that to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a correction to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: To the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meaning that it now would be again the 8th of June or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It would be the 8th of June, 1992. So the 20 July reference should removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should be taken out. I don't remember whether we discussed that before. Did we? Whatever is the case, if you are aware that there is a mistake, and if especially the range, the time range for the assessment is relevant, then take care that we have a proper translation. Apparently you were aware because you gave immediately an explanation that it still had to be done and -- okay, it's not dramatic at this moment. There seems to be a problem anyhow. The witness can't help us. But please try to do it more precise and accurate next time. After the witness has left the courtroom, we'll take a break. Mr. Jeremy, could you tell us how much time you'd still need. Also in view of -- this seems to be unrelated to the subject matter of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I estimated an hour. I'll stick to that estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question was whether it's true that it is relatively unrelated to what is found in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Malcic was a personnel officer in the Main Staff. He testified in the Karadzic case in relation to a number of these appraisals. He seems the most appropriate person to discuss the appraisals that we have in evidence with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. At the same time, time is granted to the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness, that is, primarily to test the evidence of the witness and to test it. And, of course, I know that the Rule 90(H) some room is left for asking the witness about matters which are relevant for the Prosecution's case; but whether a similar amount of time should be granted to that and whether that would not, to some extent, be an extension of the time spent of the Prosecution to present its case is a matter to be seriously reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, in your statement, from paragraph 18 onwards, you discuss the departure of non-Serbs from the VRS, and I'd like to show you a document in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3892.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, we see that this document on the screen before us is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps. It's dated the 9th of June, 1992. If we look at the bottom of the page, we see that it is signed by Colonel Milutin Vukelic. He was the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs in the 1st Krajina Corps; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, the report is titled: "Report on the Autonomous Region Krajina Crisis Staff decision," and we see that it is sent to the Main Staff and also the SR BH Presidency. You see it has operational confidential number 488-3. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in the first paragraph we read: "One of the issues that was discussed at yesterday's session of AR Bosnian Krajina Crisis Staff was the personnel -- was the general personnel policy in the Army 1st Krajina Corps." Now, in the next paragraph we read that: "Within units of the 1st Krajina Corps, there are 67 officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality." In the next sentence, we see reference to an ultimatum requesting removal of such persons from vital command posts by the 15th of June, 1992. Now, a few sentences on from there, we read: "Such action would also significantly weaken the above-named units from which it has been requested that staff be purged." Mr. Malcic, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, a sentence on, we read: "The 1st Krajina Corps command should make the decision as to which staff members from the ranks of Muslims and Croats may still be temporarily kept and at which posts." And lastly we read: "It would also be essential to take a position on what should be done with those who have not demonstrated any hostile activity so far, but who must be removed from key posts." Mr. Malcic, this is a personnel problem that the 1st Krajina Corps are asking the Main Staff to address. Now, were you aware of this purging process that is being contemplated here?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. It did not pass through my office. It is addressed to the Main Staff here of the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, I know another document that followed as an answer. Now I see that it's an answer to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether you were aware of this process as described here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malcic, you've referred to a document that you are aware of that you say was a response to this particular document, and I'd like to take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we see please see P3893.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this is an order from General Mladic to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, and you discuss this document in your statement from paragraph 18 onwards. We see that it is dated the 9th of June, 1992, so the same date as the report that we just looked at, and we see the strictly confidential number 488-3 is a reference to the number in the report that we just looked at. Do you see that, Mr. Malcic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see the teletype signature of General Mladic at the bottom of the page, and after his name we see the abbreviation SR. That means that this order was issued by General Mladic personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the text of the document we read: "Officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality must be sent on leave immediately. Take action at once to refer them to the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to resolve their status in the service." Mr. Malcic, faced with the problem of what to do with non-Serbs in the 1st Krajina Corps, General Mladic's immediate response was to send them on leave immediately. This is an example of decisive command being exercised by General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in the top left corner of this document, we read: "For Colonel Rankovic." Now, that's a reference to Colonel Miroslav Rankovic; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the first name, but I do know Colonel Rankovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he was the chief of the personnel sector in the 1st Krajina Corps; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: He was chief of the organ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness. Could he please be asked to speak into the microphone again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Rankovic was chief of the organ for organisational, mobilisational and personnel affairs in the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So he dealt with personnel issues; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in the top left of this document, we see the strictly confidential number 28/4. Now, that number relates to the personnel department in the Main Staff; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: That I do not know. I don't know whose number that is. I cannot remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at another document and see if I can refresh your memory about this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31367.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain this document? Because I took part in the realisation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Firstly we'll look at a different document, Mr. Malcic. Now, this document is dated the 25th of August, 1992, and we see your name at the bottom of the document. In the top left corner, we see the strictly confidential number 28/4. Mr. Malcic, does this refresh your recollection that this number, in fact, related to your personnel department?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Every year we got special numbers for registering documents in our personnel department. I cannot remember now whether that's the number. Probably it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go back to P3893, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: While that is being brought back on the screen, Mr. Malcic, and that's the document that the 9 June order that we just looked at, in paragraph 20 of your statement, you say that this order did not pass through your office. Now, you now believe that the 28/4 number might relate, probably did relate, to your personnel department in the Main Staff. You said that Colonel Rankovic dealt with personnel issues in the 1st Krajina Corps, yet do you still say that this document did not pass through your office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, Mr. Jeremy, just before you moved over to the other document to refresh his memory about that number, the witness said: "Can I explain this document?" I had something to do with its making, something to that effect. Which I accept would contradict his prior statement that the document didn't pass through but he does seem to recollect that he had something to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic told us in regard of P3892 that he -- that one did not go through his office. In regard of P3893, he said that he actually dealt with realisation of that document. So those are two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, can I refer your --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen D656, please; that's the statement of the witness. Can we go to page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 18, we see the reference to P3893 and you begin to discuss that in paragraph 18 and paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please, paragraph 20. Second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "This document did not pass through my office but I did know about it." So, Mr. Malcic, do I understand your evidence that, in fact, this document did pass through your office after all?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I could explain this document, how it fared, and I wanted things to be as clear as possible. I do not remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, please answer the question. Then, apart from the extensive explanation you've given already about the document in your statement, but first, did it pass through your office; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my office, I had a clerk who would log or register all the documents that left my office and that came to my office. At that moment, I was not familiar with this document. At that time, I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you were familiar with it. It can pass your office even without you knowing it. The question simply is: Did it pass through your office; yes or no? Next question is whether you saw it, whether you were aware of it, whatever may be the case. Did it pass through your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. On the basis of this number, I cannot state exactly that it had passed through my office. Perhaps it was registered in a different way and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm not asking about registration. So you say you do not know whether it passed through your office, meaning that it may have passed through your office or may not have passed through your office, you can't tell us. That's how I understand your answer; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement, you say "This document did not pass through my office." But you knew about it. So, therefore, that is a mistake. Let's leave it to that. You do not know whether it passed through your office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot understand or hear the witness. Too many microphones are on at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll switch off my microphone. Could you please repeat your answer. Could the microphone be adjusted so as to be better oriented towards the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember. I do not know that this document passed through my office. I either was not in office at the time or -- but, anyway, later, a few days later, I came across this document, and I fully familiarised myself with it, and I know how we acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then listen now, having now corrected your statement in this respect, listen carefully to the questions Mr. Jeremy will put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malcic, you provide an extensive explanation of this document in your statement, and I don't wish to go back into that in great detail. But I would like to focus on something you say in paragraph 19 where you describe it as a great favour and privilege. Now, if you were a Muslim or Croat officer in the 1st Krajina Corps, how is it a great favour and privilege to be discriminated and purged from the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: They were not being purged from the 1st Krajina Corps, they did not leave until the end of May with the Army of Yugoslavia -- I mean, into the Army of Yugoslavia in Serbia. They stayed in this army. They were supposed to be established. When we started establishing the Army of Republika Srpska, until then, they were members of the JNA. And now, certain individuals wavered. They wanted to go to Yugoslavia after they heard this information that they heard from the Crisis Staff that they were not desirable in that army. Many active-duty officers, Croats and Muslims, paid no heed to these conclusions of the Crisis Staff. They simply stayed on in their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. You say they were not being purged from the 1st Krajina Corps, and I'd like to look at a report issued by the 1st Krajina Corps four days after this --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Do allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Listen to the next question, Witness. At the end of your statement, you may add --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not answer the question. He put a concrete question to me, and I did not answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked a question. Your answer is nine lines. We consider that question to have been answered. If there's anything you'd like to add at the end of your testimony, you have an opportunity to do so, but please now focus on the next question that Mr. Jeremy puts to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, part of your last answer was that they were not being purged from the 1st Krajina Corps. Now, I would like to show you a report from the 1st Krajina Corps four days after General Mladic's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P00217 on our screens. Now, this is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps. If we go to the bottom of the page, the last page, we see that it's signed by General Talic. While we're still on the first page, we see it's addressed to the Main Staff. In fact, it's signed on behalf of General Talic. We see his type-signed signature there. Could we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, this is a regular combat report. It follows the usual formulation. In the first paragraph, we see comments relating to the enemy. In the second paragraph, comments relating to the state of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to focus on paragraph 6, state of combat morale, and that's on the next page, please. In fact, page 2 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the third sentence of paragraph 6, we read: "The purging of officers on an ethnic basis remains a topic of discussion because of the danger that it may very soon result in deficiencies in the units but it is proceeding in the spirit of the order received." Mr. Malcic, it's very clear here that General Mladic's order was very clearly understood as meaning the purging of Muslim and Croat officers from the 1st Krajina Corps; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, were you aware that at this time, thousands of Muslim and Croat civilians in Kljuc, Sanski Most and Prijedor and other areas were being removed from their jobs and their homes. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Similarly, it was time to purge any remaining Muslim and Croat officers in the 1st Krajina Corps; yes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: If I explain this to you, you will know the truth. And if I do not give you this explanation, you are going to live in this delusion and you will not know what the actual situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, once more, a gesture like thumbs up to a witness and you can follow the proceedings outside this courtroom. Is that clear to you? I'm not -- no, you were making a signal with your hand, which is impermissible, and will next time lead to the removal from this courtroom. No speaking, just listen. Witness, Mr. Jeremy puts to you three documents in a certain context. You have commented in your statement on one of them. Your comment and your description seems not to be in line with the gist of these two -- of the three documents in context. Now, if you say you are going to tell us how it was, the first thing I'd like to hear from you briefly, not a long story, why the 1st Krajina Corps sent a message saying what, after having discussed apparently the matter, how to say it briefly, how to get rid of the Muslim and Croat officers. And there's an immediate response: Send Muslim and Croat officers to Yugoslavia. And then, in a follow-up report, some concern is expressed about, at least in time following up, if we get rid of them, we might have a problem, staffing problem, anyhow, and the same language is used as in the first report, which led to the very short order to send them elsewhere. Now, that's simply the issue Mr. Jeremy is raising with you, if I understand you well, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, not tell us extensively, but how is it that this picture so clearly seems to arise from these documents and that you say it wasn't as it is -- as it seems to be on paper? If you could briefly explain that, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear the interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We didn't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where did it stop, Mr. Lukic? The interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That the whole of your last address was missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll -- I think the best thing to do would be to re-read it. When I sought verification with Mr. Jeremy, that was still interpreted? I said: "Now, that's simply the issue Mr. Jeremy is raising with you." Was that still interpreted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That part was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay, then the following part. I then asked you, could you -- and I'm puzzled, "could you tell us, but not extensively, how it is that this picture that so clearly seems to arise from these documents and that you say gives a false picture, what is it that reality was different from what it seemed to be on paper?" If you could briefly explain that, we would appreciate if you would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, four sentences. First sentence: The 1st Krajina Corps asked for the position of General Mladic what to do with active-duty officers who were of Muslim and Croat ethnicity, and some Crisis Staff insist on having that question resolved. Second sentence: General Mladic immediately responded to that document. He said officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity should be sent on annual leave for 30 days and then measures should be taken that they be sent to the Army of Yugoslavia. Why 30 days? So that these active-duty officers who are ethnic Muslims and Croats should give this serious thought, what they should do further on. When they were asked by the Army of Yugoslavia to stay there, to join them, they stayed in the garrisons of the 1st Krajina Corps. That's where they had apartments, that's where their wives had jobs, and that's where their children went to school. Some of these officers immediately said that they would stay in the Army of Republika Srpska. Another group of people said that they were staying in the Army of Republika Srpska. They consulted their family members, their children, because this is a major turning point in the families' lives. Those who decided to go into the Army of Yugoslavia, because the Army of Yugoslavia was the successor of the JNA, and until then, they had been members of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they would be sent to the Army of Yugoslavia. Those who wanted to do that gave -- got motor vehicles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I stop you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- they loaded their moveable property --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and they went and joined certain garrisons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, I stop you there. Witness, you said four sentences. You've now taken a whole page and you are moving away from what I asked you. The issue is why, on paper, it is presented as how do we get rid of them? And how is it that, on paper, it is not, and that's apparently your explanation, let's give them free choice. Let's give them time to consider all that. That's not what the papers say. The papers give a totally different explanation. And I asked you what explains the huge difference between your interpretation of the situation and the interpretation of the situation as we find them in those documents? If you have an explanation for that, rather than to explain again what your view is, you can give it. If you don't have an explanation for that, Mr. Jeremy will put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that I am supposed to explain this document written by General Mladic. General Mladic provided his position, his opinion when asked. It's not an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Listen, you misunderstood that and you are not invited to further do anything else than I asked you to do. And apparently you have no explanation at this moment, not of the document, but of the contradiction between your version and the version as it appears on paper. Mr. Jeremy, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, your comments in your statement in relation to this 9 June order from General Mladic and the comments that we have heard in the last few answers you provided to this Chamber focus on officers in the 1st Krajina Corps; correct? Muslim and Croat officers.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: If you allow me. That was the only document that was in writing asked by the 1st Krajina Corps and according to this document, we acted in all the other corps and the air force and air defence because there was no unit at that point which did not have any Muslim and Croat officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you again. The question is: Was it about officers, just about officers? That means not soldiers, not non-commissioned officers. Was it about officers? Your statement and your explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army that had remained in the units of the VRS together with us Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, it is correct, is it not, that at this time, it wasn't simply officers of Muslim and Croat ethnicity who were being removed from their posts in the VRS. In fact, it was all active-service personnel who were being removed from their posts; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who wanted, after the JNA withdrew from Bosnia, to remain in Bosnia remained. The other troops and a large number of Muslim and Croat officers from the JNA deserted from JNA units and joined the new armed forces being created by Croatia and the Muslims. Those who had remained at that time were rare Yugoslav-oriented people who wanted to defend Yugoslavia as much as we did, like we, the other officers of the JNA who remained until the end in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, what I'm asking you is whether at this time -- I'm no longer referring to officers, so the non-officer class but I'm asking whether active military personnel of Croatian and Muslim ethnicity were removed from the VRS at this time during these June, July months?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I think the question has been answered, to some extent, by the witness where he said they deserted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not removed, those who remained until the last day. They remained in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please see a final document, Exhibit P4971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By re-reading, I do agree that the witness was then talking about officers again, although you had guided him away from officers. But apparently he disagrees with your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, before I take the witness through this particular document, I am aware of a typographical error. I've sent it for -- we've made a request that it be corrected. And that error is the -- where we see reference to our strictly confidential number 28/4 and then it goes on to contain a date. In the original mit's 9 June 1992, and in the translation it's 9 July 1992. So we're dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Malcic, we see that this is a document from the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential number 28/4, and it's dated 9 July 1992. The heading is: "Regulating status in service of active-duty military personnel." We see a reference to our strictly confidential number 28/4, 9 June 1992. That's the document -- that's the 9 June order that we looked at earlier. Now, we read in the text of this document -- excuse me, before I read it out, we see it it's type-signed General Mladic. We read in the text of the document: "On returning from annual leave, refer all active-duty military personnel of Muslim or Croatian nationality to the personnel administration of the General Staff of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for the purposes of regulating further their service status." Now, I also draw your attention to the strictly confidential number 28/4. That's the number that we were discussing earlier in respect to the 9 June document, when we were discussing whether or not that passed through your office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now could we go to the second page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are working on the translation anyhow, then also correct the number 23 in the top which, in the original, reads 233. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, we see a list of who this order is sent to. And you'll agree with me that that's the entirety of the VRS, correct, in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this order, sent to all active-duty military personnel of Muslim or Croatian nationality, did you consider this and do you consider this particular order to also be a great favour and privilege intended for the protection of these soldiers in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Those who decided after 30 days not to remain in the Army of Republika Srpska, it was not said in the first document where they should be sent. This is an addition to the previous document. It is said that they should go to the General Staff of the JNA, and they -- their status, a new assignment, would be decided based on their training and competencies. It was an advantage compared to the Serbs because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not only slow down. But, Mr. Jeremy, put a question to the witness not as you did, ask for the purpose of all this. Witness, listening to your answer, it seems that you're focussing very much on those who -- that had decided not to remain in the army, whereas the document makes no distinction between those who had decided to remain or not to remain. But carefully listen to Mr. Jeremy's next question which will be more -- no, listen to the next question, Mr. Witness, Mr. Malcic. Mr. Jeremy, of course, with the question you put to the witness, you can expect an answer which does not stay within what you would like the witness to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, you'll agree with me that this document relates to all Croat and Muslims, the remaining Croats and Muslims, serving in the VRS and it gives them no option to remain in the VRS as of 9 July 1992. You will agree with that.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: You put it very well, active, active military personnel, not reserve personnel. And I was a professional officer who dealt only with active-duty personnel. Those active personnel who decided, after 30 days, to remain -- not to remain were directed to go to the General Staff. Those who decided to remain, remained. Which means a large part of these officers remained in the VRS. There was no purge. The rest were directed to go to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions on this document or on this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Have the questions by Mr. Jeremy triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe just to finalise the last sentences witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Malcic, you said a large number remain in the Army of Republika Srpska. Is there any record of that in the personnel department, in the archives of the VRS, currently the archives in Kozara?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I don't know where this archive is, but I know that until the end of the existence of the VRS, a large number of active-duty Muslim and Croat officers remained in the Army of Republika Srpska, and most of them were in the air force and air defence. That was according to the rules of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, just answer the question. The question was whether, in the archives, currently the archives in Kozara, whether there's any record of that personnel remaining. Is there a record in the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be the order governing the continuing service of these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know whether there is, I understand, although you think there should be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that while I was in active service, I made some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was not well put. Is the archive of the Main Staff in Kozara; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I left on 31st August 1997. After that time, I don't know what happened in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you want to ask the witness something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point, I think you said you had spoken to General Mladic about this. Can you tell us briefly what was said in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: When this order was sent to units, their professional organs called me up and asked, Why should we send these officers on leave when nobody has the right to go on vacation at this time? So I went to General Mladic and asked him. And he answered, to the best of my recollection, You will agree that it is a huge decision for every family what your future would be, to go to somewhere -- some place unknown or remain here, which is your home, and you did not join the national parties when everybody did and you did not go to the JNA when the JNA was inviting. Some people who were then in the army did not find it convenient because they believed they could -- because some of our officers thought they could create their own Serbian state without us, and that order was made to deal with these extreme people, and I personally liked it. I thought that innocent people should not be harassed, that they should be enabled to decide wherever they think they will be better off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think we saw two orders -- or not orders, whatever the witness tells us about it, the one is to send them to Yugoslavia, the other one is that, upon return, they had to report to the -- okay. So in your question it was unclear which order you referred to. Second, could you tell us exactly where the witness said that he had spoken to General Mladic about "this," apart from what "this" exactly was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say it anywhere in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, I had a conversation with Mr. Lukic, not with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just discussing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I had this conversation with my colleague Stojanovic, and obviously I was confused with my conversation with the witness, and he confirmed, Mr. Stojanovic, that it was not mentioned today on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if there's anything relevant in your conversations with witnesses, put it on paper, bring it to our attention in that way. So the witness may have said that but not in this court and not -- it doesn't appear in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just clarify regarding which opinion of Mr. Mladic he was talking about, as you wanted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if you withdraw the question, I do not have to know about which one it was. You're referring to something the witness has said. You established that he has not said it. Therefore, I'm not insisting on any further clarification at this moment. Put your next question to the witness as you deem fit about this or about any other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would still like to ask you, when you discussed this, was it in June or in July? When did you speak to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is "this"? I earlier said that it's unclear when you talked about the order which one was meant and that, therefore, when you discussed "this" is as unclear as a result. Now, in your question, you again say: "When you discussed this." Discussed what, Mr. Lukic? That should be clear before the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But even before that, you said "discussed with General Mladic," which you have established never took place, never mentioned in this court. And Judge Orie said he doesn't want to hear any further about that one. So the discussion with General Mladic, which this witness has never referred to, doesn't become a topic for discussion at this point because, first, it doesn't even arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I think it did arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This witness has never said in this court that he discussed with Mr. Mladic. This is introduced by you and the Presiding Judge made a ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously inartfully raised by me. I could ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then that is ruled out by the fact that it doesn't arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we have -- even the document I wanted to ask whether the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Much depends, Mr. Lukic, whether it's about the document you have introduced through the statement or whether it's about any document. Because the document you introduced in the statement, you can't say that it arises from cross-examination because it finds its origin in this statement you've taken yourself and the document you've referred to yourself. Now, therefore, I insist on what is it about that you want -- what is "this"? What is the document? And if that results in any testimony of the witness that he has discussed it with whomever, we'll hear that. But what document are you referring to? The one you introduced in your statement or one of the documents introduced with this witness by Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think not to be on the wrong side, if you can ask the witness which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't. I don't have the basis for putting any such question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may consult with my client just for a half a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may consult your client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The voice of Mr. Mladic is by far too loud for consultation purposes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Malcic, did you discuss with General Mladic personally and at what time the issue we discussed in the previous session, that is to say, the document on "differentiation" of the Muslims and Croats who are members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The document sent to Colonel Rankovic personally was written or dictated by Mladic himself. It didn't go through me. That document was not clear to Colonel Rankovic. He called me the next day, on the 10th of June, and asked, Why should these officers be sent on annual leave when nobody else is going? I said I will ask General Mladic the first chance I get. I don't know how many days passed after that, one, two or three, but I eventually met General Mladic and asked him why. And in response to my question, he said what I just described. He said, People need 30 days to think seriously, to consult with their families, because it is a huge change in everybody's life. They have the right to go to the Army of Yugoslavia because the Army of Yugoslavia accepts all officers of the JNA who stayed in the JNA until the last day they were in Bosnia. And he didn't send them off to join their national armies. He treated them very humanely. He gave them time to think about it very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're going beyond the question. The question was - and you have answered that question - that you discussed the matter with General Mladic after the order apparently was sent to Colonel Rankovic and that an explanation was given to you which is similar to what you told us and which, as we established before, is not in line with the other documents dealing with the same problem and that is of some concern. Next question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, if the witness would have discussed this conversation with Mr. Mladic in any of the conversations with you, it's totally not understandable why you have not raised the matter in your examination. And, second, why you have not sent any proofing note which relates to that. It comes as a surprise in the third --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not at this moment, and I just make this observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because he didn't -- he never told it to me while I was preparing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whatever the defence, whether it's you or whether it's Defence, I leave that open. You took the statement at the time. I think you were the one. So then that also comes perhaps as a bit of a surprise that it is not in there. But if it call came at the last moment, told to anyone else, then still the question remains why you did not raise it in the examination-in-chief which -- because it seems to be pretty relevant for the matters discussed with this witness. I leave it to that. Have the questions in re-examination triggered any need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, but I would like to emphasise that as issues like this arise, then it's vitally important to the Prosecution that we become aware of them at the earliest opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that it's one of the few times that no additional questions were put to the witness, apart from summarising the statement, and it now turns out that it was one of the -- certainly one of the circumstances in which it would have been helpful to immediately be aware of that. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to say something to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No problem. I just wanted to say, Mr. Lukic, if in re-examination, you remember something that you didn't raise in in-chief, the proper procedure is just to request the Court if you may raise it and offer the Prosecution the opportunity to re-cross-examine on that new issue. That's the proper procedure. Rather than just push it in and say I can explain. This would give the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you request that you raise the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: By mistake, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there are no further questions for the witness. Mr. Malcic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague -- yes, I offered you an opportunity to add at the end anything you wanted to add and that opportunity is given now. But, please, it should relate to any of the questions that were put to you. Is that clear? And it should be short. You have an opportunity to add whatever you deem necessary to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never appeared before any court ever, except here in The Hague. This is the second time. I said something before this Court after the question put by the Prosecutor and then it reminded me of some of these things in relation to this document. Nobody had asked me about it before. And that's why I thought I should say this, because I thought this was the right place where I should say things that I happened to remember and that I should say it under oath. I do apologise, once again, if I did anything that was inappropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have two versions: The one that you raised the matter of your conversation with Mr. Mladic with the Defence; and the second version now being that you remembered it only after questions had been put to you by the Prosecution. I leave it to that at this moment -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't understand me. They did not understand me -- they did not ask me anything before, and that's why I didn't say anything. I'm saying that I remembered it all today when I was asked these questions by the Prosecutor. Had they asked me before, I would have said the same things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic has explained to us that similar things were said earlier in your conversations with the Defence, that is, about your conversation with Mr. Mladic, and that was what I was focussing on. This concludes your testimony. I have thanked you for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for having heard me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We went a bit beyond our usual time. After the break -- first, do we have to deal with associated exhibits at this moment with this witness? Because I do understand that from -- for the previous witness that we will discuss it somewhere next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For this witness, is there anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer those two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Lukic, if you would give their numbers in sequence, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first one is 1D2440. It's exchange of JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2440 receives number D657, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D657. Next one, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And actually next one is already in the evidence under the P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's only this one. Then having dealt with that, Mr. Lukic, may I take it that the Defence is ready to call its next witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- yes, I nevertheless would like to deal with one matter briefly. It will not take more than five minutes but I'd like to have dealt with it before the break. And we have to -- need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break and we resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. It's Mr. Vlade Lucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I further draw the attention of Mr. Mladic to the following. There was not only communication with gestures, Mr. Mladic, with the witness which I said would lead to measures to be taken. Similarly, you have an active interaction by gestures with the public gallery which is also not acceptable; and, therefore, if that continues, a screen will be put between you and the public gallery so that everyone can -- in the public gallery can see you on their monitors, and you will be unable to communicate in the way as you did before the break. Let that be clear to you that that would be the measure to be taken if it continues. Then finally, I, Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Lukic, D657 -- Mr. Lukic is not there. But I started saying that D657 was admitted into evidence. Then something came in between, but D657 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lucic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
