utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text of a solemn declaration will be handed out to you now. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lucic. Please be seated. Mr. Lucic, you will first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to have 65 ter number 1D04015 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look on your monitor, do you remember giving this written statement to the Karadzic Defence team in 2012?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could please turn to the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the last page in the Serbian original, can you please tell us whose signature appears at the end of the statement.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: My signature is at the end of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, subsequent to signing this statement in 2012, did you have occasion to review the same in the Serbian language so as to ascertain if everything was correctly recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that opportunity. I read it and everything was written the way I had stated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I were to ask you questions today about the very same topics as contained in your statement, would your answers be the same as recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes. My answers would be the same as those contained in the statement, but perhaps the word order wouldn't be exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, since you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, would that mean that the testimony as contained in your written statement is truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my knowledge, everything I said in this statement is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I tender 65 ter number 1D04015 as the next Defence Exhibit. We do not tender the three associated exhibits that are mentioned in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4015 receives number D658, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D658 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time, I have a written -- I have a summary of the written statement that I'd like to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Lucic is a retired career army officer. In May 1992, he received orders to report to the Sarajevo Corps, then still called the JNA 4th Corp., and was assigned to the 216th Mountain Brigade under the command of Colonel Dragomir Milosevic. He was ordered to take over command of an infantry battalion. The witness was the commander of the 2nd Battalion from 18 May 1992 to the end of January 1993, at which time he moved to the command of the 1st Romanija Brigade. Upon taking command of the battalion, he immediately noted that the lines were not covered with enough men, that the defence was not linked, and that establishment weapons were lacking. On 22 May 1992, the 1st Romanija Brigade was formed. The strategy and objectives of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in relation to Sarajevo was to prevent the penetration of the BH army into Serb territory. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps mainly conducted defensive operations due to the lack of manpower, while the BH army units were almost always on the offensive. He and his unit were aware of the international conventions that protect the civilian population in war, so they opened fire in self-defence, and only against military targets. He recalls that the VRS Main Staff and the Serb civilian authorities extended offers for Sarajevo to be completely demilitarised, with all heavy weapons to be placed under UN control. The Serb side also took a liberal stance with regard to freedom of movement of civilians both toward and from Sarajevo. And that completes the summary of the witness's written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any further questions for the witness, you may put them, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that, Mr. Ivetic, can I just -- at line -- page 52, line 11, 10 to 11, you're saying that -- the witness was moved in January 1993 to the command of the 1st Romanija Brigade. Then you followed that by saying "upon taking command of the battalion..." Do you mean to say the brigade or the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The battalion, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Is that referring to the previous paragraph when he became commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It refers to this paragraph where it talks about the time-period when he was commander of the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I would have some additional questions for you. First of all, I would like to ask you if your battalion had any mortars?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the battalion had mortars. At first, it was less, and later, more were added. However, the level never reached that that had been envisaged by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what calibre mortars you had and how many.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: In the battalion, there were 60-millimetre mortars and 82-millimetre mortars. 60-millimetre mortars were within companies, whereas 82-millimetre mortars were a separate unit, and it was called the independent platoon of 82-millimetre mortars. It was within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have enough personnel to man --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the second part of the question was not answered; that is, how many. The witness explained to us where they were within the battalion but ... Could you tell us how many all together 60-millimetre mortars there were in the companies and how many 82-millimetre mortars there were in that separate unit, and at what point in time? Because I do understand that initially you had less and later you had more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer now? When I assumed my duty, as far as I can remember, there were two 60-millimetre mortars in two companies respectively. And in the battalion, in the independent platoon, there weren't any 82-millimetre mortars because that platoon was still in the process of being established. There was a platoon commander, a deputy commander, and a few soldiers, as far as I can remember, because their command had issued the following order during mobilisation that that platoon should be manned only by reservists, that is to say, military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I was not asking about who were in those platoons. I was just asking about the number of mortars. I do understand that when you assumed duty, there were 60-millimetre mortars, two mortars in each of the two platoons. The 82-millimetre mortars, could you tell us when they then arrived in the separate unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 82-millimetre mortars, they arrived -- well, I cannot say exactly what the date was, but it was during the month of May or the first half of June, there were two 82-millimetre mortars. Otherwise, according to establishment, there should be six mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you talk about June, is that June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the number of mortars increase since then or decrease, either the 60-millimetre or the 82-millimetre batteries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both numbers increased. In that area, in addition to this nucleus that I took command of, after mobilisation, companies were established, and then one company got two mortars of 60-millimetres, whereas the 82-millimetre platoon was later on replenished with another two, and then, at some point in time, in September, another two. So that was six all together. And during the month of October, the platoon was relocated to the village of Podgrab or, rather, Nikolici. The slopes on the south-east of Jahorina. So that is the opposite side of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that, in total, there was six 82-millimetre mortars at the end of 1992. What was the total number of the 60-millimetre mortars at that point in time or at its highest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time, there were already six 60-millimetre mortars, two respectively in all the companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you tell us about how these mortars were planned to be used by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The mortars were within the combat disposition of the company as one element of that disposition, and they were planned to be used within the assignment given to the unit, and that assignment was to defend that stretch of the front line and that area as well as the population that lived behind the lines near defence positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you also tell us how it is that they were used to defend the lines? What kind of fire missions did they undertake?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Mortars did not have any firing mission. They were there and they had to be ready to be used, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when would they be necessary to be used, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the use of weapons was gradual, depending on the disposition, that is to say, in case of attack on the line or part of the line, those who were forward would fire first, and then if that was not sufficient, then the commander would use the 60-millimetre mortar with a proviso that the direction and the range of those mortars was strictly regulated. It's what we called the forward-most line of defence, that is, the firing line that is behind cover, and the order given to the commanders is to use mortars only when there is no other way just in front of the defence line or if a trench line had been reached by the enemy, then to use mortars to defend the trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you please explain for us, you said, "in front of the defence line or if a trench line has been reached by the enemy then to use the mortars to defend the trench." In the case of mortars being used in either of those instances, what area would be targeted by those mortars?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The line of defence in that specific area where I received my battalion leaned on the Miljacka river, from Vrbanja to the next bridge on the Miljacka, and then towards the stadium. And, on the other side, it was from the intersection near the Vrbanja bridge towards the Spomen park. So in front of the defence line, there was a belt of 60 up to 100 metres that was clear. That was the river and sometime the promenade. It was a clear area, and they could use the weapons in this belt if they were unable to prevent an attack by the enemy differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where were the enemy forces situated in relation to this clear belt of 60 to 100 metres that you have identified?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The assaulting forces were directly opposite on the other side of the Miljacka river. In the beginning, they were just behind the Vrbanja bridge behind a wall or they were also using some buildings there, but they also covered a part of the promenade that was looking from the infantry line. On the flanks we were separated from the enemy only by one street that ended at the stadium. On the other side near the Vrbanja bridge, there was a large intersection, and on the side towards Spomen park, they were very close, behind a building, sometimes at a distance of only 30 metres. I did not tour every single trench but that was roughly the disposition of defending and attacking forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, did the mortars in your battalion ever get repositioned so as to shoot into the interior of Sarajevo beyond this belt that you have identified?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: While I was commander, the mortars did not change position and never fired behind the lines, never find into the depth behind this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to take a look at your statement which we have on the screen, and I'd like to look at paragraph 5 at the bottom of both versions. Here you say that there were not enough men to cover the line. Could you explain for us what types of things you did in order to be able to cover the line with insufficient manpower.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The general situation in my battalion and in the brigade was a shortage of personnel. We built trenches, not all of which were occupied, and we often had to take part of the personnel from units and during the night take them to those positions where an attack was expected, and we deployed these men behind a cover to pre-empt an attack on the defence line. We did not have a line defence because, for us, it was a resisting type of defence. We did not plan withdrawal, so our defence was deployed in depth and along the entire line, I had men and assets deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you able to cover the entire defence line?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, we were not. We changed cover from time to time, and since my battalion was practically semi-encircled and behind the lines, I was surrounded by firing positions across Vrace, that's an area they controlled by snipers, it's an area where you would move only by night and under cover. So I was encircled, in firing terms, and I was in a semi-circle as far as the enemy forces are concerned. These attacks came not only from the front but from the flank, and I would sometimes have to take men away from the first line and take them to the flanks towards Mojmilo hill, the Ozrenska Street to link them up with a neighbouring unit, or take them perhaps to the area overlooking Spomen park called Zlatiste where we often had to intervene with infantry. So all the forces that I had at my disposal were engaged to the maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I please seek clarification of one of the previous answers and perhaps of the question as well. You were asked, Witness, whether the mortars in your battalion ever got repositioned so as to shoot into the interior of Sarajevo beyond this belt that you have identified. And then your answer was that they did not change position and that they never fired behind the lines. My question is, if you would, hypothetically, want to fire beyond this belt, would there be a need to reposition them? Or could, from their positions, could be fired into the interior of Sarajevo? Not to say that it happened, but I'm just asking you whether from the positions, as unchanged, whether it was possible or impossible to fire into the interior of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the positions where the mortars were, it was possible to fire into the depth in the interior, and I see that you frequently use here the term "at the city." To us professionals, those were just forces of the 1st Corps that attacked us. We fired only at them. But, tactically speaking, they were able to fire into the depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The very last line of your answer puzzles me again. You say "tactically speaking, they were able to fire into the depth." My question about -- was about your ability, and I do understand that you were able to hit targets, as you explained, forces of the 1st Corps, if they were situated in the city, that at least your mortars were able to engage such targets beyond the lines within the city. And I'm not suggesting that they did, but I'm just trying to understand both the question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Distinguished Mr. President, I'm not quite clear as to what you imply by my ability to fire at the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said we fired only at this -- this belt and not beyond that. My question is whether your mortars could have fired beyond that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies in advance. I have to be more precise. I didn't say that we fired. I said that the mortars were planned for use in that area in case infantry weapons were not sufficient to stop an attack. A mortar from that position had the technical and the tactical possibility to fire several kilometres into the depth, but it never happened because it was not within our assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there was no need to reposition there if you would have wished - and I'm not suggesting that wish existed - if you would have wished to fire into military targets within the city.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, there was no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How often and in what manner would the enemy forces attack the defence line that your battalion was defending?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: You could classify these attacks as classical or partial. They were daily and sometimes nightly. But if you narrow this definition only to the use of their mortars along the entire line and assault groups from flanks and from the front, such attacks were very frequent, especially in the period of end May, the month of June, and the month of July 1992. I'm talking about the period when I was the commander of that unit until January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how would the enemy forces move toward the line, toward the defence line?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: They built fortifications and, whenever possible, they dug trenches and built covers. During the night, they approached and combat groups approached frequently, destroyed a certain cover and advanced their own line. That was accompanied by a mortar attack against the rest of the defence units or by sniper fire or other infantry weapon fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you tell us what were your orders that you received in respect to your interactions with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The first orders regarding UNPROFOR we began to receive in the month of June notifying us of the upcoming arrival of UNPROFOR units, informing us that they would probably have control of the airport, but the main point was that we had to convey this order down to every single soldier. That UNPROFOR was able to move wherever they wanted, to cross any bridge they wanted, and that we must not interfere with their mission, and we must prevent any individual or group trying to interfere with them. That was an order that every soldier had to be familiarised with, and the brigade commander said that he would personally check that it is done when he toured the positions near the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, sir, what were the orders given to your unit by your superiors in relation to the passage of humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that any humanitarian convoys passed across Grbavica. But the order was that we must not interfere with it, that they, as a humanitarian organisation, were doing their job, and we were not supposed to intervene or hinder them in any way. And, second, since these units were being reinforced by conscripts that had escaped from Sarajevo, they were very motivated to see that humanitarian aid actually reached the city. And through those humanitarian organisations, they personally sent some assistance to their relatives and families that remained in Sarajevo. And one of my company commanders asked for permission to send a package occasionally through those humanitarian organisations, a package containing food or clothing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask about the meetings which you attended at the command of the brigade. What kinds of instructions were given in relation to the treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the first part of your question. Did you say something about the brigade or the command?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At the time that you moved from the level of battalion commander to the role you had in the brigade command, and when you attended collegium -- pardon me, meetings at the command of the brigade, what kind of instructions were given by the brigade as to the treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: You are narrowing down my answer. It's not only that we got orders from the brigade command. The way the army treated the civilians is well known. You know where the core of our unit was; it was the 216th Mountain Brigade. It was made up of people who had done their military service, who had been members of the Territorial Defence or the civilian protection, and some reserve police units. All of them had been mobilised. And from the very beginning, it was quite clear what the mission of the army was: To defend the area and to defend the population. And it was constantly stressed throughout their training. Nobody, except authorised police officers, had any powers over civilians, no right to search their apartments, to search them, to harass them, et cetera. If there was a need to intervene, sometimes, in cases where there was a problem, the commanders were supposed to inform the competent organs, that is to say, the military and civilian police, and leave it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What kind of instructions were given as to the disciplining of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Just to add one thing about civilians. It was clear, since this was a populated area, it was emphatically prohibited to stop civilians, to enter apartments, to appropriate property, or commit any other criminal act. When soldiers needed to be disciplined, there were measures prescribed by the law. For minor infractions, disciplinary measures applied, and for more or less serious crimes, the competent authorities were notified and criminal complaints were filed. I remember since we had a detailed briefing where all the members of the commands, that is to say, assistant commanders, made reports about the previous period, the assistant commander for security reported that he had for the previous period already filed 17 criminal reports. I don't know to what they referred because in my unit, nothing like that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My final question, and perhaps you've already answered it with your last line. Did you your battalion have any such incidents requiring criminal or disciplinary proceedings against its member soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it had. The first problem was going AWOL. Individually or as a group, soldiers would sometimes leave and go without permission to their homes. They would be taken into custody by the military police and commanders would in such cases pronounce disciplinary measures. At one briefing, one of the commanders reported disciplinary problems with one soldier, and I said, Bring him to me. And since this soldier constantly displayed disobedient behaviour, questioned the commander and undermined him in other ways, I pronounced the measure of two days in detention because that was within my powers. Another case happened in June. Upon returning from leave, a platoon commander did not take his platoon to the positions according to regulations causing strong infantry and mortar fire, resulting in one death and seven wounded. Since the platoon was already small and it had lost one-third of the men, that commander had to be dismissed. His rank was stripped, and he was integrated into the neighbouring platoon as a private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm -- you used until now a little bit over half an hour. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I prefaced this as my last question so once the witness is finished, then I'm complete with my direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I did, and he was in the middle of answering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was in the middle of answering it. Yes, Witness, you explained a lot about disciplinary action taken against those who apparently had disturbed the internal order and internal functioning of the forces. If that is what you wanted to ask him, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could just follow-up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's giving examples, and I don't know for how long he would continue to do that. So if you have any further question or any focused question on the matter, please put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you: In your battalion, were there any criminal proceedings that were required against any of the soldiers for criminal behaviour?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Apart from the few cases that I just described that were dealt with along the chain of command, there were certain cases that involved crimes and criminal liability had to be dealt with. The army filed criminal complaints -- reported such cases to the competent authorities and criminal complaints were filed. Such cases were rare. One of them happened in August in a company whose positions faced Vrbanja bridge. I don't know exactly how the investigating authorities dealt with it. I'm just describing how I learned about it by the company -- from the company commander through his reports. A soldier tried to stop a civilian who was entering a building. The man continued to move. The soldier caught up with him and asked to see an ID. And the man hit the soldier whereupon the soldier opened fire. Another soldier who tried to stop his colleague got fired at too. I know that there was a trial. The man was convicted, but I don't know any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Apart from firing at the civilian and another person, one of whom survived, the other didn't, the soldier committed a violation, first of all, when he insisted that the civilian show his ID. He should have reported it to the authorities. The building the civilian was trying to enter was just behind our positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before we go into further details of this event, do you remember what the ethnicity of the person was who slapped the soldier in the face and was then shot at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, but I think it's a Bosniak or Muslim. And the other one was either a Serb or a Croat. I don't know, the other civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you have any name of the victim or victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whatever I say is to be the truth, as I said, but I cannot say anything now with 100 per cent certainty. I think that the name was Ilija, but this is really with a reservation that that is what I seem to remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ilija as a first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, first name. But really, with the reservation because I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you for answering my questions today for the Defence of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we take the break first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that you'll start your cross-examination after that. Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. President. The topic that was just discussed was a bit outside the scope of the statement and the summary. If it's possible to just ask one question of the witness before the break and that would give us an opportunity to develop cross-examination on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that would be fair. No objections, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, who is counsel for the Prosecution, will put one question to you. Then we'll take a break, and after that, she'll continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lucic. I wonder if you remember the name not of the victim of the incident you just spoke about but of the soldier that you alleged was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Prosecutor. I remember the last name of the soldier, I do not remember his first name. His last name was Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And to clarify, Mr. Ivetic had asked you about your battalion specifically. Was this a soldier in your battalion, the 2nd Mountain Infantry Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was in a company or, rather, a squad within a platoon within a company within my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And my final clarification. You spoke about August. Are you referring to August 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first take a break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we wait for the witness, if I can ask for Exhibit P4621 to be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, in your statement, and today during your testimony, you made several claims about the 1st Corps of the ABiH having greater numerical strength than VRS units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer you to paragraphs 7, 8 and 16 of witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you able to see the document on the screen in front of you, Mr. Lucic?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is a 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade command reply to the SRK command dated 16 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please have page 2 in both versions of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to refer you to an item under number 3 of the document. On the B/C/S, it is the first bullet on the page that is now on your screen. In the English, it will be the last bullet on page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now we have both in English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now for the English, I think we still need the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In English, it's page 2 focussing on the bottom of the page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: While that's coming up, I will tell you what this document states is that: "Manpower levels of the brigade command consisted of 80 per cent senior officers already at the beginning and subsequently reached 90 per cent, whereas manpower levels of the battalion commands are 100 per cent, including all key command positions." Mr. Lucic, according to this report, the battalion commands under the brigade command, including your battalion, were at full manpower levels as of September 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Ms. MacGregor asked for page 2 and not for page 3. Now we are at page 2. Lower part. Yes, could you answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer. What is written is correct. The battalion command was manned and that was just the command. If you allow me, I can tell you who makes up the command, that is the commander, his deputy commander, then the assistant commander for security affairs, and then the assistant commander for logistics, and then the desk officer for atomic and biological warfare, and then the signals people who are not part of the command. That would be it. So this is not a reference to units but to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can move on. I'm going to be looking now at -- I think it's page 1 in each document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if you can wait, I haven't yet asked a question.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I wanted to answer the question that you've already put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question that was put to you has been answered and the new question is still to be expected. Wait for a second. Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now looking at the first page of this document, focussing on paragraphs 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, in your statement at paragraph 10, you state: "The SRK mainly conducted defensive operations due to a shortage of manpower." Now, if we look at the first paragraph on the document in front of us, it reads: "The brigade command is 'consistently carrying out the instructions on the persistent safeguarding of the lines reached to date and the bringing about of the conditions for offensives' ..." Mr. Lucic, is it correct that as of September 1992, the brigade command was planning to conduct offensive operations?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: In September, I was in the command of the battalion; I was the commander. But the brigade and corps had defence establishment. This is a reference to the creation of conditions for offensive activities which is a general tactic and strategy of the Army of Republika Srpska to always defend themselves successfully and possibly carry out offensives, if so planned somewhere. And over here, it is a reference to units that should exist for carrying that out, if necessary. It says here that we are firmly holding our positions with these forces but the conditions are being created. Conditions are being created. That means --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We only sit in court today until 2.15 and I am doing my best to use that time efficiently. If you can please just answer the question that's put to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I no longer need the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, during your testimony in the Karadzic trial, you were asked a question by the Prosecutor and you were asked about the brigade. You testified that in your brigade: "Ammunition was used strictly in a professional manner." And the transcript reference for that is Karadzic, page 30797. Do you stand by that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Additionally in your statement, Exhibit D658, in paragraph 24 you state that there was no misuse of ammunition, at least not in your unit. Now, by "unit," are you referring to the brigade or are you referring to the 2nd Mountain Infantry Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Well, battalion, first of all, and then in 1993 when I was transferred to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So this statement refers to your knowledge about both your battalion and the brigade in general as you continued to be part of the brigade command through the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of your statement, you refer to how members of your unit, under your command, opened fire in self-defence and only against military targets. Can you again clarify what you mean by your unit under your command?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The battalion that I commanded, because in the brigade, I was a professional organ and the brigade was commanded by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can I please have Exhibit P4440. We'll be on page 1 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: While we wait for the document to come up, Mr. Lucic, this is a warning dated 19 July 1995 from the SRK corps command to several brigades, including the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. Now, I want to focus on the second paragraph of this document. The first sentence of that second paragraph relates to problems with ammunition production. despite these problems, SRK forces continued to "spend ammunition as if we had it in abundance." The second sentence of this paragraph states: "That is why we very often fire at inhabited settlements and specific buildings where there are no combat actions whatsoever." Moving to the next paragraph: "It is inexplicable that some brigades spend much less ammunition in repelling three or more fierce attacks during the day than others that fire at inhabited settlements when there are no combat actions." Now at the time that this warning was issued by the SRK corps command, you were no longer assigned to the 2nd Mountain Infantry Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I don't see the date here when this order was issued. I cannot see the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can have page 1 of the B/C/S version. And to explain to Your Honours and to Defence counsel, the 65 ter number -- excuse me, the exhibit number includes four pages. The first two are the telex version of this document. The second two are the version that was signed by Milosevic. They're identical in every other way in terms of the text. If you look here on the first page of the first version of the document, the telex version, you see a handwritten note of the date, and this is reflected in the English translation on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's translated as 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Let me just -- no, you're right. I made mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, do you see on the first page the handwritten notation of the date, that it seems to say July 19th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see this is not typewritten. A pen was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Is it correct that on that date, you were no longer assigned to the 2nd Mountain Infantry Battalion, which you referred to in paragraph 11 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, I was within the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can please have 65 ter 31339, English page 11, B/C/S page 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, what's coming up on your screen is a document you were shown before during the Karadzic testimony. It's a range table for a 60-millimetre mortar. And I'm going to turn to the page that deals specifically with the range for the fourth charge. Now, if we look at the bottom left of the chart on the B/C/S version, would you agree, Mr. Lucic, that the maximum range is listed as 2.538 metres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: On the very bottom left-hand corner of the B/C/S version of the table, the last number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was looking at the English, which is very small.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: May I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you agree that that is what the chart reflects?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Down here, I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please adjust your microphone slightly so as to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I see it in the first column, 2538.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31339 receives number P6791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And the Prosecution no longer needs the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, before the break, you referred to a proceeding against a soldier with the name Pejanovic for shooting a civilian. During the break, the Prosecution conducted a quick search of our records of SRK personnel and did not find a soldier with the last name Pejanovic. The Prosecution did find a record of a soldier for the ABiH with the last name Pejanovic. Do you recall if the soldier that you were discussing before the break was Serb or Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Soldier Pejanovic who fired, well, we did not keep records of ethnic affiliation but he was an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you saying Bejanovic, starting with B, as a boy; or Pejanovic, starting with P, as in pirate?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: P. P. That soldier was within the 216th and he stayed on within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, the Prosecution searched with a misunderstanding that it was spelled with a B so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and if we are talking about P or B, Paris, I think, in both languages would give the clue to the right letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Lucic, is it correct that in your battalion, specifically your battalion, there were no actual prosecutions for violations of international criminal law?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: No, not in my battalion. While I was commander, no, there was not a single case. I'm sorry, maybe I answered a bit too fast. Could you tell me what you mean exactly by that? There were crimes. There were violations, but at any rate, nothing went unpunished.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: By "prosecution," I'm referring to an investigation and a criminal trial proceeding similar to the setting that we're in right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that perhaps not the use of the word "prosecutions" may have triggered the problem for the witness but, rather, the words "violations of international criminal law." I take it by the way that these are violations of international law, although criminal acts -- what Ms. MacGregor apparently is referring to is crimes which are -- do exist in relation to the international law of warfare, that is, attacking civilians, abuse of prisoners, well, that type of what we find in the Geneva Conventions and what we find in other international instruments regulating warfare. So that's, apparently, I understand Ms. MacGregor was referring to. Do you know of any prosecutions of any military men within your battalion for such violations of the international law of warfare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. In my unit, the unit I commanded, the battalion, there was not a single case of any violation of these provisions of international law, and no one was tried before an international court or a national court in that sense, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you now about your assignment after January 1993. In paragraph 6 of your statement, you state that the command of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade changed locations several times. Is it correct by the time that you were moved to the brigade command at the end of January 1993 it was located at Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I was transferred in the beginning of February to the brigade command. At that time, or before that, the barracks of the 216th Mountain Brigade of the JNA was the barracks in Han Pijesak. However, when mobilisation was carried out, so that was earlier on -- so at that time, that part of the brigade, except for part of the logistics, was in the territory of Lukavica, that is to say, eastern Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can you please answer just the question. Where was the brigade command located as of February 1993, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: In February 1993, the command of the brigade was in the area between Pale and Han Derventa where the road to Sarajevo and Sokolac forks off, so perhaps about 17 kilometres away from Sarajevo in some facility that was called Alpina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And at what point was it relocated to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: When the brigade left its home barracks, as it were, in 1995, it was never again retransferred to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My question was when was it first at Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: We are talking about two structures of the brigade. Han Pijesak was the location of the 216th Mountain Brigade of the Yugoslav People's Army until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm putting up my hand because we have a lot of evidence already on this topic. And what I actually want to clarify, in the interest of time, is were you outside of Sarajevo starting in February 1993 until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: The brigade command was outside of Sarajevo but one part of the units was located there, facing the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My question was about your location from February of 1993 until the end of the war. Not the location of different parts of the brigade command but you personally.

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: I personally was in the Alpina building between Pale and Han Derventa. From Pale to Han Derventa is 7 kilometres, and the Alpina building is halfway. And Han Derventa is 16 or around 16 kilometres from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the Karadzic trial, transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- before we -- Mr. Stojanovic, if we want Mr. Mladic to speak at a low volume, then you should come closer to him rather than to keep on your earphones and receiving from a distance what he says by far too loud. So that's my instruction for you. Ms. MacGregor, would you have any indication as to how much time you would still need because we are at a point where we have to adjourn soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One final question. And then we'll see whether Mr. Ivetic has further questions and whether we could extend the session in such a way so that the witness could return before the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the Karadzic trial, transcript reference 30796, you testified that once you moved to the brigade command in 1993, you were "mostly focused on organising defence towards Gorazde and the Nisici plateau." Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that term "organising" is something I would not accept. The defence was already in existence but not in full. There were some areas that were not defended, so it was a question of organising units to defend such areas. It was not that I was organising something anew. And that was, of course, on the orders of the commander. He specifically directed me to that battalion whose command was in Podgrab to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained that you used the word "organising" as not setting up something from zero but that it was busy with the continued organisation of. Any further questions, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would potentially have just one or two questions, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest to all of those supporting us to assist in a briefly extended session so that the witness, who would otherwise have to stay over until Monday, could return home. I see no one jumping up. I hear no major complaints. Well, no loud speaking under whatever circumstances, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've told that we have no problem with continuing the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's appreciated, especially if that is what Mr. Mladic brought to your attention. I exceptionally would accept loud speaking under those circumstances. Please put that one or two questions to the witness, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please call up again Exhibit P4440.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, sir, I can refresh your recollection. This was the document dated July of 1995 that was shown to you by Madam Prosecutor, the warning from the SRK commander. And I want to ask you, sir, at this date, did the line of defence of your brigade include or face Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: At the time when this document was written, the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade did not have this front line of defence facing Sarajevo. It had changed its location, that is to say, its area of defence, and was in the Nisic plateau area with its corps forces directed at the forces from Tuzla, Zenica, that is to say, the 1st Corps of the BH army. The line of defence faced Vares and Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered your question. So, therefore, you could intervene. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next question. Were there any populated areas in the line of defence as -- that you have just described to us?

utterances.speaker: VLADE LUCIC
utterances.text: Ahead of that line, half of the area of defence faced a forested mountain area of Mount Zvezda, and another part faced hills and grazing fields where there were villages but they were only partially populated at that time. That's where the line went through. Ahead of us where we were firing, there were no populated areas or civilians. There was nothing apart from the enemy army that was launching that very strong offensive with the objective of linking up with its corps in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think the witness now goes beyond your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was waiting for the translation to complete. And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you again, Colonel, for answering my questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you to everyone for the indulgence of a few -- ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, any questions? The Bench, Mr. Lucic, also has no further questions for you. Therefore, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties or by the Bench, and I would like to wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, but not after having thanked all those assisting us for making it possible for this witness to return home before the weekend. It's really highly appreciated. We will resume Monday, the 29th of September, 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of September, 2014 at 9.00 a.m.
